Automation across the estate

Admin → Automation. One page for both kinds and every background run on the install.

The two older pages — job runs, and scheduled — redirect here.

Two kinds, named by where the work runs

Section titled “Two kinds, named by where the work runs”
Scheduled task Job
What runs An HTTP request to a path the app published, in the app’s own process A command, in a process of its own, with its own memory limit
The app must be Running Not necessarily — a batch app has no process at all
Needs Nothing background_jobs_enabled, and somewhere to run — a cluster, or this machine
Limits Tight — the ceiling and the memory envelope are the boundary Generous

They are named by where the work runs, never by trigger. Both can be scheduled; both can be run on demand.

Where a job runs

Section titled “Where a job runs”

The install decides, once, and an app’s own mode is never consulted.

  • Where isolated execution is available, a run is a pod in the cluster, as it always was. Every install that ran jobs before keeps doing so.
  • Where it is not — no cluster — a run is a process on the platform’s own machine, started by launchpad runner (the platform binary itself, so a host run and a pod speak one contract) as a process group of its own under the app’s OS account. It gets a directory of its own for its identity and scratch, removed when the run ends. It is not PM2, whose memory limit is a restart, and for a job a restart is a second run nobody asked for.

Admin → Settings says which applies, under Background jobs: Runs execute in the cluster or Runs execute on this server, with a sampled memory limit. Each run records the mode it actually ran in.

Caution

On this machine, the memory limit is a watchdog, not a wall. The platform samples the run’s process tree every couple of seconds and kills it past the limit, recording a resource-exceeded failure so the kill cannot read as an ordinary one. Between two samples a run can allocate past its limit, and on a machine with no headroom the kernel chooses the victim — which may be the platform. A run that outlives a platform restart runs on, unwatched, under its deadline alone. If you need the limit guaranteed, that is isolated execution.

On an install that can never isolate an app, the Settings page leaves out the rows that only govern isolated apps — Background jobs, New apps are born and the two CPU figures — rather than showing them disabled. The Isolated execution row stays, and says why.

Batch apps: only jobs

Section titled “Batch apps: only jobs”

A batch app is an app whose only entrypoints are jobs — a nightly extract that does not need a web server it would never answer. It is declared, never inferred, by a [batch] table in launchpad.toml, because a Go main, a Python main.py and a Node start script look exactly like web apps to every detector. Node, Python, Go and R only; [batch] beside [static] is refused.

What differs for you:

  • No service. Dependencies install as for the language’s web apps, and the deploy skips the start and ready steps. The flip to the new release is the whole of going live.
  • Its status is ready, not running: nothing answers, so nothing is running. If you alert on app status — in the telemetry launchpad.apps.by_status metric, say — an alert written as “not running” now counts batch apps. Write it against the statuses you mean.
  • Restart and Stop answer 409 no_service, and a scheduled task cannot be created on one (it serves no path). The app’s address shows Runs jobs, and its page has no Open, Start or Stop.
  • Locking one writes no stopped — there is nothing to stop. Its runs are its workload, and the lock cancels them (see below).

A batch app can still send mail and notifications from its jobs; see Sending from a job.

Schedules, in a zone

Section titled “Schedules, in a zone”

A schedule of either kind is UTC unless it names a time zone — CRON_TZ=Europe/London 0 6 * * *, or the Time zone field on the dialog, or a timezone key beside schedule in launchpad.toml. Lists print expression · zone. A prefix typed into schedule in a manifest is refused: one way to say it in a file.

It fires once per wall-clock time, across daylight-saving changes. A 06:00 London job runs at 06:00 in both seasons. A time that falls inside the spring gap is moved forward by the gap; a time that occurs twice in autumn fires once. The cron library was measured and refused for this, because it skips one day and fires twice on another. Zones resolve the same on any image, because the zone database is compiled into the binary.

A run knows the instant it is for

Section titled “A run knows the instant it is for”

Every job run can carry scheduled_for — the tick it belongs to, not the moment it was dispatched. A run that waited an hour behind its app’s queue limit still knows it is the 03:00 run. The job receives it as LAUNCHPAD_SCHEDULED_FOR, written in the schedule’s own zone, and a retry carries its original’s.

A manual run has none unless a person names one — lp job run --for, or the Run for dialog — because defaulting to now would make a re-run of last Tuesday quietly process today. An app starting a job itself is acting now and cannot set it.

Overdue, skipped and failed are three different reports

Section titled “Overdue, skipped and failed are three different reports”

All three are recorded on the app’s events, mailed to its owner under the usual failure-notification rules, and resolved by that job’s own next success — with a recovery notice that names the job.

Event Means Raised
job_run_failed / cron_run_failed A run ended badly. By the run. Non-manual runs only.
job_schedule_skipped A scheduled firing was refused by the queue — the app already had as many runs in flight as it is allowed. When the firing is refused. The schedule has already moved on, so without this the run would vanish with only a log line.
job_run_overdue A job has gone expect_within without a success. By the jobs sweep.

expect_within is set in launchpad.toml or the job dialog — a duration such as 26h or 7d, from one hour to 31 days. It is for work nobody watches: a job that fails already sends a notice, but one that stops running — paused and forgotten, refused by its queue limit, never placed — sends nothing.

  • Succeeded, not finished. A job failing every night is already reported and would otherwise be reported twice.
  • The window starts at the later of the last success and the moment the job was enabled, so a new or re-enabled job is not overdue on arrival.
  • A disabled job is never overdue — a pause is somebody’s decision, and alerting on it teaches people to ignore the alert. Nor is a locked app’s.
  • One stuck job is one event. The sweep skips a job that already has one open.
  • On a manifest job it is the repository’s, like schedule; an edit in the UI is the same 409 pointing at the repo.

A lock is the one refusal not recorded as skipped: the lock is the explanation, and it is shown wherever the app is.

One automation’s success resolves only its own failure. Earlier, an hourly job succeeding closed — and mailed a recovery for — a failing nightly one in the same app. Failure fingerprints now lead with the job or task, and a recovery names it: The job “nightly-extract” is succeeding again.

A locked app runs no jobs

Section titled “A locked app runs no jobs”

Locking an app stops its jobs as well as its workload, whichever of the two lock sources placed the lock (you, or the dependency policy):

  • a scheduled or manual start is refused;
  • a run queued before the lock is cancelled when it comes to be dispatched;
  • a run already running is cancelled by the jobs sweep.

Sending from a job

Section titled “Sending from a job”

A job holds no app token, and nothing in its environment opens app data, viewer identity or job starts. It may do one thing on the app surface: send through the integrations attached to its app, so notify in an SDK works inside a job — which is what lets a batch app mail its own report.

The run’s own token is accepted on /api/v1/app/notify/*, /deliver/* and /sends/* only while the run is in flight. Anywhere else it is a 403 job_send_only, and after the run ends it is a 401 run_not_in_flight. The integration gate, the send ledger and the idempotency window apply exactly as to the app’s own sends, and so does your attach: a job reaches only what you attached. Jobs still cannot start jobs, so one compromised job is not an amplifier.

Who can read job history

Section titled “Who can read job history”

A job’s definition, its run list, and a run’s detail and logs are readable by the log audience — people who can edit the app — and no longer by anyone who can merely read it. A run’s parameters, result, actor and output are workload output, and a viewer, or an anonymous visitor to a public app, must not see them any more than they see the app’s logs.

A run executes the release it was queued against

Section titled “A run executes the release it was queued against”

A run queued behind a deploy runs the release it was queued for, not whichever is current when it starts. If release retention has since removed that release, the run is refused by name rather than quietly run against a different one.

Provenance is shown

Section titled “Provenance is shown”

Where a schedule came from — launchpad.toml or the UI — is on the listing.

launchpad.toml is optional and still the better door: it travels with the code and is reviewed with it. An app with no manifest still has the UI.

The caps

Section titled “The caps”
Setting
job_concurrency_per_app How many of one app’s runs may be in flight. Over it, a refusal the SDK names.
max_run_retries The ceiling on how many extra attempts an automation may ask for. 0 turns retries off everywhere.
max_scheduled_tasks_per_app Counted per schedule rather than per endpoint.
scheduled_task_timeout_seconds Past this the run is a failure.
scheduled_run_result_bytes How much of the app’s response is kept. 0 stores none.

Retention for runs and logs is in Retention.

The rules that keep automation honest

Section titled “The rules that keep automation honest”

A retry is opt-in, unattended-only, and never silent. A scheduled run can retry; one somebody started by hand does not, because they are watching. Every retry is visible as a retry.

Parameters are never interpolated into a command. A parameter cannot become part of a command line, which is what makes it safe to let somebody else supply one.

One claim, two tables. A run is claimed once; there is no double execution under contention.

Stranded runs are reconciled. A killed runner’s run does not stay running forever, and the checks page’s stuck work row finds what the reconciler has not.

A skipped run is recorded; a refused one is not. A task that could not fire — the app was stopped, locked, or the previous run was still going — is a record with a reason. A request refused before it was a run is not. (A scheduled job firing the queue refuses is the exception that proves the rule: the schedule had already moved on, so it is recorded — see Overdue, skipped and failed.)

An app starting its own work

Section titled “An app starting its own work”

An app can start a different entrypoint of itself, never another app, and it never asserts who a viewer is — it relays a platform-signed token.

These routes take a run id, so the ordinary rule applies: an app can only reach the runs it started.

When automation stops

Section titled “When automation stops”

In order:

  1. The checks page — stuck_work and scheduled_tasks; and the app’s events, for a job reported overdue or skipped.
  2. This page — is the schedule there, is it enabled, when did it last run.
  3. The app — is it locked (a locked app runs no jobs), stopped, or crash-looping.
  4. The dials — is max_run_retries zero, is job concurrency at one.
